parties:
Ali Miah @ Ali Akbor and others Defendant-respondent-petitioners
VS
Safuler Nessa and others -------- Plaintiff-Appellant-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
(a) 8 annas share as to 'Ka' schedule property of CS khatian No.70 comprising 23 decimals of land, 

 (b) 202.50 decimals of land as to Kha schedule property of CS khatian No.280 (94 decimals of land in Plot Nos. 3443, 3450 and 3480 as exclusive possessor and 108.50 decimals of land in rest of the plots in 8 annas share, total (94 + 108.50) = 202.50 decimals of land), 

 (c) 16 annas share as to `Gha' schedule property of CS khatian No.678 comprising 94 decimals of land, and 

 (d) 8 annas share as to `Gha' schedule property of CS khatian No.813 comprising 78 decimals of land. 

 3. The properties situate at mouza Sreepatirchar, Police Station-Homna, District-Cumilla. The basis of the abovementioned claim of the plaintiffs, as stated in the plaint, is that CS khatian No. 70 was recorded in the names of the plaintiffs' predecessor Uzir and the defendants' predecessor Wahed Ali in equal shares. Plot Nos. 3443, 3450 and 3480 of CS khatian No. 280 were recorded in the name of Uzir Ali as exclusive possessor and the rest of the plots were recorded in the names of Uzir Ali and Wahed All in equal shares. CS khatian No.678 was recorded exclusively in the name of plaintiffs' predecessor Uzir Ali. CS khatian No. 813 was recorded in the names of Uzir Ali and Wahed Ali in equal shares. Uzir Ali died leaving behind the plaintiff No. 1 Montaz Uddin alias Momtaz Uddin as only son and two daughters namely, Sabaner Nessa (plaintiff No. 2) and Moina Bibi. While the son and two daughters of Uzir Ali had been possessing the scheduled property as owner through succession, Moina Bibi died leaving behind Toyfol Nessa (plaintiff No.3) as only successor. The plaintiffs have been possessing the land in ejmali by erecting houses and growing crops. The schedule mentioned properties were not partitioned which have resulted in misunderstanding and quarrel between the parties. On 19-4-2008, the defendants refused to partition the property amicably and hence, the suit for partition. 

 5. In respect of CS khatian No.70 (Ka Schedule) and CS khatian No.813 (Gha schedule), the defendants do not dispute the plaintiffs' case that these-khatians were recorded in the names of Uzir All (plaintiffs' predecessor) and Wahed All (defendants' predecessor) in equal shares. 

 6. In respect of CS khatian No. 280 (Kha schedule), the defendants claim that the said khatian was prepared in the names of Uzir Ali and Wahed Ali in equal shares. Subsequently, Uzir Ali sold and handed over possession of 17 decimals of land in plot No. 3443 and 14 decimals of land in plot No. 3450, both of CS khatian No 280, total 31 decimals of land to Wahed Ali, but no registered sale deed was executed. On 21-11-1944, Wahed Ali transferred the said 31 decimals of land to his wife-Arabia Khatun through a registered deed of hiba-bil-ewaj. 

 7. In respect of CS khatian No. 678 (Ga schedule), the defendants' case is that although 94 decimals of land of the said khatian were owned and possessed by Uzir Ali and Wahed Ali in equal shares, but during the CS operation the same was wrongly recorded in the name of Uzir Ali. During the SA operation, the land was correctly recorded in the corresponding SA khatian No. 815 in the names of plaintiff No. 1, who is the son of Uzir Ali and these defendants as successors of Wahed Ali in equal shares. 

 10. The trial Court held that out of 397.50 decimals of land of the four khatians as claimed by the plaintiffs, they are entitled to saham of 303.50 decimals of land in the following manner: 

 from CS khatian No. 70 in 8 annas share = 23 decimals 

 from CS khatian No. 813 in 8 annas share = 78 decimals 

 from CS khatian No. 280 in 8 annas share = 155.50 decimals 

 from CS khatian No. 678 in 8 annas share = 0.47 decimals 

 11. The plaintiffs preferred an appeal which was allowed in part. The appellate Court below modified the decree passed by the trial Court by enhancing the saham of the plaintiffs from 303.50 decimals of land to 350.50 decimals of land. In so doing, the appellate Court allotted the entire land of CS khatian No. 678 (94 decimals) to the plaintiffs while maintaining equal shares in respect of the rest three khatians to the plaintiffs and the defendants respectively as allotted by the trial Court. 

 13. Mr Md Mostafa, the learned Advocate for the defendant-respondent-petitioners, submits that he has no objection as to allocation of saham to the parties in respect of CS khatian Nos. 70, 813 and 280 by the appellate Court below. The learned Advocate, however, submits that the appellate Court below committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice by allotting the entire share of CS khatian No. 678 to the plaintiffs inasmuch as in the corresponding SA khatian No. 815 the names of the plaintiff No. 1 and these defendants were recorded in equal Shares which cast cloud upon the title of the plaintiffs so far as entire share of CS khatian No. 678 is concerned and therefore, until and unless the plaintiffs' title in the entire share of CS khatian No. 678 is declared by a competent Court or the corresponding SA khatian is not declared wrong by a Civil Court, the suit for partition simpliciter is not maintainable. In support of the argument, the learned Advocate refers to the case of Rezaul Karim and others vs Shamsuzzoha and others, 49 DLR (AD) 68. 

 14. Mr Sikder Mahmudur Razi, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellant-opposite party Nos.1-16, on the other hand, submits that it now settled principle of law through judicial pronouncement that in a suit for partition, the Court can determine each conflicting claims incidental to partition. In support of the argument, the learned Advocate refers to the cases of Shashi Kumar vs Nagendra Nath, 1982 BLD 36 and Cinmoy Chowdhury and another vs Mridul Chowdhury and others, 55 DLR (AD) 115. The learned Advocate next submits that order VII, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers the Court to give relief to the plaintiff as he is found entitled to but omits to pray. The learned Advocate refers to the case of Dhaka City Corporation and others vs Shamsur Rahman and others, 59 DLR 207 in support of the argument. The learned Advocate further submits that the appellate Court below rightly allotted the entire share of the land of the CS khatian No. 678 to the plaintiffs as the same was recorded in 16 annas share in the name of the plaintiffs' predecessor and that there is no basis of recording 8 annas share of the same in the defendants' name in the corresponding SA khatian. In this regard the learned Advocate submits that the presumption of correctness as to CS khatian is not available with regard to the SA khatian. In support of the argument, the learned Advocate refers to the cases of Akrab Ali and others vs Zahiruddin Kuri and others, 30 DLR (SC) 81, Hindu Devi Lakshmi Gobinda Jew vs Deputy Custodian Enemy Property (now vested property) Government of Bangladesh and others, 7 BLT 133 = 51 DLR 300, Hriday Ranjan Dey and another vs Niranjan Dey being dead his heirs, Probate Dey and others, 10 

 16. In the instant suit for partition, the plaintiffs prayed for saham of land in respect of four CS khatians. Both the trial Court and the appellate Court below allotted 8 annas shares of land of three khatians to the plaintiffs. The bone of contention arises in respect of CS khatian No. 678. Plaintiffs claimed 16 annas share of land of CS khatian No.678, but the trial Court gave 8 annas share to them which, on appeal filed by the plaintiffs, was modified and the appellate Court gave 16 annas share of land of CS khatian No. 678 to the plaintiffs. Now, the defendants are the petitioners before me. 

 17. Admittedly, 16 annas share of CS khatian No. 678 was prepared in the name of the plaintiffs predecessor Uzir Ali. Defendants claim that the land of CS khatian No.678 was owned and possessed in equal shares by the respective predecessors of the plaintiffs and the defendants. So, the CS khatian No. 678 was wrong which was corrected in the corresponding SA khatian No. 815 which was recorded in equal shares in the names of the plaintiffs and the defendants. 

 18. The trial Court observed the plaintiffs failed to prove that neither their predecessor nor the plaintiffs are the owner, and possessor of the entire land of CS khatian No. 678. The trial Court further observed that in the corresponding SA and BS khatians, the land has been recorded in equal shares in the names of the plaintiffs and defendants which prove that the defendants own and possess 8 annas share of land of CS khatian No. 678 as successors of their predecessor. However, the trial Court did not elaborate its findings with reference to any oral or documentary evidence. The appellate Court below reversed the finding of the trial Court holding, 

 “এই সম্পত্তিতে (referring to CS khatian No. 678) বিবাদীর মালিকানা অজর্নের কোন প্রমাণ বিবাদী উপস্থাপন করেনি । এস, এ, খতিয়ান কোন ভাবেই মালিকানার প্রমাণ বহন করেনা । ... স্বীকৃত মতে বি, এস, খতিয়ান এখনও চূড়ান্ত হয়নি। ...সুতরাং সাক্ষ্য বিশ্লেষণে এটাই প্রতীয়মান হয় যে, ৮১৫ নং এস, এ, খতিয়ানে ভুল রেকর্ডের সুযোগে ওয়াহেদ আলীর ওয়ারিশগণ (বিবাদী-রেসপনডেন্ট) ৬৭৮ নং সি, এস, খতিয়ানের মালিক উজির আলীর সম্পত্তিতে ভিত্তিহীন হিস্যা দাবী করছেন। এই ৬৭৮ নং সি, এস, খতিয়ানে বিবাদীর কোনরূপ মালিকানা নেই। অর্থাৎ সি, এস, ৬৭��� খতিয়ানের সম্পূর্ণ ৯৮ শতক সম্পত্তিতে ওয়ারিশসূত্রে উজির আলীর ওয়ারিশগণ (বাদী-আ্পীলকারী) একক মালিক মর্মে প্রমাণিত হয়। বিজ্ঞ নি্ন আদালত কোন ধরনের প্রমাণ ব্যতিরেকে এই খতিয়ানের অর্ধেক যা ৪৭ শতক ভূমিতে বিবাদী রেসপনডেন্ট এর মালিকানা আছে মর্মে যে সিদ্ধান্ত দিয়েছেন তা সঠিক হয়নি ।” 

 19. The learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners could not show that the findings of the appellate Court are perverse or that appellate Court misread the evidence or that it failed to consider the evidence, which if considered, the findings would have been otherwise. In Halima Begum and others vs Syed Ahmed and others, 21 DLR 854, it was argued that SA khatian having recorded the disputed land in the name of the pre-emptor it should be presumed that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in respect of the said disputed land. It was held, 

 "It is true that record of right indicates certain right of certain parties but that right is certainly dependent on some material evidence, oral and documentary so as to establish title in favour of persons who claim under the said record of right. The presumption of correctness as to CS record of right is not certainly available with regard to the State Acquisition Khatians. There is no presumption of correctness in respect of the State Acquisition Khatians as it is to be found in case of CS Khatians in pursuance of the provision under section 103-B of the Bengal Tenancy Act." 

 "The presumption of the CS Khatian under section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is that every entry in a record of rights finally published shall be the evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to he incorrect. Reference may be made in this regard to the case of Akrab Ali and others vs Zahiruddin Kari and others, 30 DLR (SC) 81." 

 21. Reverting back to the case in hand, the defendants could not show as to how their predecessor became owner of 8 annas share in the land of CS khatian No. 678. The entire land was recorded in the name of the plaintiffs' predecessor alone. Therefore, I am of the view that the appellate Court below rightly held that the plaintiffs are the owners of 16 annas share in the land of CS khatian No. 678 as successors of the CS recorded owner Uzir Ali. 

 22. I have already noted that the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners has. argued that the instant suit for partition is not maintainable due to the fact the SA khatian No. 815, which is corresponding to CS khatian No. 678, has been recorded in the names of the plaintiffs and the defendants in equal shares as owners. Thus, a determination of the respective title of parties is required which cannot be adjudicated in the suit for partition simpliciter. The learned Advocate has relied upon the case of Rezaul Karim and others vs Shamsuzzoha and others, 49 DLR (AD) 68. In the reported case, it has been held as under: 

 25. In Md Sultan Mia and others vs Hazera Bibi and others, 1984 BLD (AD) 23, it has been held that a question of title can incidentally be gone into a partition suit. The cases of Rezaul Karim and Md Sultan Mia were discussed in Cinmoy Chowdhury and another vs Mridul Chowdhury and others, 55 DLR (AD) 115 wherein it has been held that in a suit for partition all the incidental questions of title, however, complicated it may be, can be decided and finally disposed of. The parties should not be thrown away or driven out on the ground of maintainability of the suit and, as such, the argument as to non-maintain-ability of the suit perishes without any footing. In Cinmoy Chowdhury, it was further held, 

 26. In the instant case, the plaintiffs proved their title in respect of 16 annas share in the land recorded in CS khatian No. 678. The appellate Court below categorically found that the defendants failed to prove their title in respect of 8 annas share in CS khatian No. 678. Therefore, the instant partition suit is maintainable inasmuch as no dispute emerges as to the title of the plaintiffs to the partible property and that the title of the parties can formally be determined to effect partition. 

 27. The trial Court found that earlier the plaintiffs filed objection case under section 30 of the Bengal Tenancy Act in respect of plot Nos. 2934 and 3042 of CS khatian No. 678 which was rejected. This finding is a total misreading of documentary evidence. Records show that the said objection case was filed in respect of plot Nos. 3443 and 3450 of CS khatian No. 280. Therefore, this finding, which is wrong on the face of the records, does not assist the defendants.

2. The facts necessary to dispose this appeal are that the appellants and respondent Nos. 3 and 4 as the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 612 of 1977 in the Court of Munsif, third Court, Narail (now the Assistant Judge) for declaration of title to the suit land on the averment that the suit land originally belonged to Abhoy Charan Bhattacharay and Prabol Chandra Bhattacharaya, two full brothers under erstwhile landlords, Babu Dhirendra Nath Roy and others at a jama of Rs. 13/1/3 paisa and was recorded and finally published in their names in CS Khatian No. 348 of mouza Bhowakhali. Subsequently, Abhoy Charan Bhattacharaya died leaving behind his only son, Manindra Nath Bhattacharaya who also died unmarried leaving behind his uncle Prabol Charan Bhattacharaya as his heir and thus, Prabol Charan became the sixteen annas owner of the suit land. Prabol Charan later died leaving behind his only son, Harendra Nath Bhattacharaya as his heir who had been impleaded in the suit as pro-forma defendant No. 3. Harendra Nath Bhattacharaya gave oral settlement of the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs on 7th Magh, 1355 BS corresponding to 21-10-1949 on receipt of an amount of Rs.1,500 as salami at an annual rental of Rs. 10-00 and granted receipts for those. Ever since the settlement, the plaintiffs had all along been in continuous and peaceful possession of the suit land for long over twelve years and thus, had also acquired statutory title by adverse possession. During the last rent roll operation, the suit land was wrongly recorded in the names of Harendra Nath Bhattacharaya and deceased Manindra Nath and in such circumstances, the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 204 of 1976 in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Narail and the suit was decreed ex-parte in their favour. Thereafter, on the basis of the said decree, the plaintiffs went to mutate their names by filing an application before the Circle Officer (Revenue), Narail and from the report of the Tashilder concerned, as submitted to the Circle Officer (Revenue), it came to the light for the first time that the suit land was enlisted as enemy property. The defendants had no title or possession in the suit land but out of greed of grabbing the suit land, they filed Miscellaneous Case No. 367 of 1969 in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Narail under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the Act, 1950), but when the plaintiffs, on being added as parties, filed written objection, the defendants had created two forged kabalas, purportedly form Harendra Nath Bhattacharaya and Manindra Nath Bhattacharaya through false personation. The former had left this country and settled in India long ago and the latter died long ago. Late Manindra Nath and Harendra Nath were railway employees in India and never executed the kabalas. When the plaintiffs on the basis of the decrees obtained by them, went to mutate their names and filed an application for that purpose, they came to learn that in the meantime, defendant Nos. 1 and 2 had managed to get their names mutated on the strength of their forged kabalas and the Circle Officer (Revenue), Narail refused to allow the mutation in the names of the plaintiffs on 2-11-1977 and being emboldened thereby, defendant Nos. 1 and 2 on 8-11-1977 denied lawful title of the plaintiffs in the suit land, giving rise to the plaintiffs' cause of action and hence the suit. 

 3. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that Harendra Nath Bhattacharaya and Man indra Nath Bhattacharaya gave oral settlement of the suit land in favour of defendant No. I at a salami of Rs. 1,500 and at a rent of Rs. 10/4/annas on 18th Magh, 1358 BS and granted a receipt for the amount of salami and rent. But during preparation of the rent roll, the record at the preliminary stage was prepared in the names of Manindra Nath and Harendra Nath Bhattacharaya whereupon defendant No. I filed an objection under section 19(1) of the Act, 1950, but the same was rejected. Subsequently, he filed Miscellaneous Case No. 367 of 1969 in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Narail for correction of the record under section 143A of the Act, 1950 and the question of title having been involved the said case was withdrawn. Thereafter, for avoiding complication, he obtained two kabalas, one in his name and another in the name of his wife, defendant No. 2, from Manindra Nath and Harendra Nath who themselves executed the kabalas. Subsequently, on the basis of the said kabalas, they mutated their names. The settlement in favour of the plaintiffs was forged, fraudulent and ante-dated. The defendants initiated a proceeding under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against the plaintiffs which was made absolute. The plaintiffs had brought this suit on false allegations in collaboration with certain persons of Bhowalkhali. The suit was barred under the principles of estoppel, waive? and acquiescence and limitation and was also bad for defect of parties and, as such, the same was liable to be dismissed.

In the report it has been stated that the gifted land of the petitioner's grand father was never a private property according to the record. 

 10. The Headmaster of the Alexander Model Government Primary School issued a letter dated 29.04.2013 where it requested guideline from the Upazilla Sikha Officer regarding the Donor Member as the land is khas land. 

 12. Suddenly, the respondent No.3 on behalf of the respondent No.2 issued a letter vide Memo No. Prasia/5P/16Bidda-Chotto/2009/913 dated 15.7.2013 and stated that there is no scope to include any member of land-giver in the Managing Committee of Alexander Model Government Primary School as the land is khas land and therefore the gift by the petitioner's grand father was not a valid one. 

 17. Mr. Amit Talukder, learned Deputy Attorney General along with Mr. Md. Jahangir Alam, Assistant Attorney General appearing on behalf of the respondents submits that .24 decimals of land in plot No.7619/8297 in JL No.18 of Char Alexander Mouza Ramgai Upazilla under District Lakshmipur has been recorded in khas khatian No.1 of the Government and it was finally published in P.S. record of 1935 and in remarks column of the khatian it was written as school. In S.A survey of 1960 also the said .24 decimals of land of plot No.7619/8297 was also recorded in khas khatian No.1 of the Government. They have further submitted that in this regard the grand father of the petitioner was not the owner of the said land. As per land record the school is situated as khas land and Government is the owner of the land. They have also submitted that the respondent No.3 legally and lawfully issued the impugned letter as per Nitimala dated 15.11.2012 and, as such the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 19. It also appears that the Surveyor of the Upazilla Land Officer, Ramgati, Lakshmipur in pursuance of Memo No.10 dated 18.04.2013 submitted a report dated 25.04.2013 to the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Ramgati, Laxmipur, wherein it is clearly stated that one Abdur Rahman Munsi son of late Rahim Uddin Patwary, Village-Char-Alexander, Mouza No.1 of Char-Alexander, in Khatian No.1 and dag No.8297 by a registered deed No.1459 dated 12.08.1935 gifted 0.24 acres of land in favour of the President of District School Board, Noakhali which was recorded as Char Alexander High School on 21.07.1996. Misc Case No.01/1933-34 and on the basis of N.H. Misc. Case No.01/1933-34 the said .24 acres of land was recorded in his name and gifted said .24 decimals of land to Char Alexander Primary School.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the instant Rule are that on 19-6-2005 the predecessor of the opposite-party No. 1 as pre-emptor filed an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 being Miscellaneous Case No. 23 of 2005 before the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Bagharpara, Jessore for pre-empting the case land measuring 5 decimals appertaining to SA Khatian No. 39, Plot No. 626 (old), and No. 951 (present) of Mouza Dogachhia under Police Station Bagharpara, District Jessore. 

 4. The case of the pre-emptee-petitioner is that without cause of action the case is bad for defect of parties, barred by limitation and the case land along with other lands originally belonged to three brothers, namely Bhejal Mondal, Sharat Mondal and Bharat Mondal in equal shares and SA Khatian No. 34 was correctly prepared and finally published in their names. Bhejal Mondal died leaving behind one daughter named Laxibala Bhoumik as his sole heir. Thereafter Bharat Mondal died behind his brother Sharat Mondal to succeed his estate and then Sharat Mondal died leaving behind his widow and the preemptee as his heirs. Out of necessity for money, the mother of the pre-emptee mortgaged 37 decimals of land from the case jote to Amullya Sarker and Bijoy Krishna Sarker by a registered deed of patta and subsequently, SA record was prepared in the name of the said Amullya Sarker and Bijoy Krishna Sarker. Although the mortgage money was repaid, a redemption deed could not be executed due to financial crisis of the pre-emptee and his mother. The SA Khatian prepared and published in the name of Amullya Sarker and Bijoy Krishna Sarker is erroneous and the pre-emptee had no knowledge about the said khatian. The pre-emptee is in possession of 49 decimals of land in the case jote by inheritance and as such he is a co-sharer in the same. The pre-emptor had full knowledge about the impugned sale and that he has no necessity to pre-empt the case land and thereof, the application for pre-emption is liable to be dismissed. 

 5. The pre-emptor examined 2 P.W.s including himself as PW 1 and the pre-emptee cross-examined them in detail. The pre-emptor exhibited the impugned sale deed dated 2-6-2005, SA Khatian No. 39 and the sale deed dated 22-1-1995 as Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 respectively. Although the examination-in-chief of the pre-emptee as OPW 1 was recorded in part, he did not turn up before the trial Court to complete his remaining examination-in-chief, the cross-examination and accordingly, no other documentary evidence was produced by him to substantiate his defence case as contended in his written objection.

full_judgment:
2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present petitioners as plaintiffs instituted the original Title Suit being No. 78 of 2006 in the Court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Satkhira Sadar for declaration of title and further declaration that the S.A. record is wrong with an additional prayer of partition contending inter alia, that the suit properties appertaining to C.S. khatian No.771 of Mouza Madhabkhali under P.S. Satkhira originally belonged, to one Enamul Hoque Biswas comprising an area of 54 decimals of land under whom one Bagan Behara Sarder was a korfa tenant and the under khatian was 773. Due to arrear of rent for non-payment of the same by the korfa tenant Bagan Behara the landlord preferred a rent suit and obtained a decree therein. Thereafter, in decree Execution Case No.221 of 1952 the property was auction-purchased by the landlord and subsequently decided to settle with the land. The plaintiff's father namely Madar Sarder at a salami of Taka 50/- and yearly rental of Taka 5/- took settlement of the property. In favour of the landlord Enamul Hoque Biswas Madar Sarder executed a registered kabuliyat in respect of the land on 25.02.1956. Thereafter; Madar Sarder out of the total 54 decimals of land sold out 10½ decimals of land in favour of the defendant No.5 and delivered possession. Subsequently; by another transfer deed dated 31.10.1966 Madar Sarder transferred 8 decimals of land in favour of one Abdul Khaleque who by a subsequent transfer deed dated 17.12.1990 transferred that 8 decimals of land along with other lands in all 27 decimals in favour of the plaintiffs No. 1 and 2. Madar Sarder died leaving behind four sons Abdus Salam Sarder and others, one daughter Anwara Khatun and wife Meherful bibi. In this way the plaintiffs are possessing the suit land by way of inheritance and their purchase deeds. During S.A. operation due to ailing condition of Madar Sarder his brother Nur Mohammad was entrusted responsibility to record the name of Mather Sarder, but Nur Mohammad Sarder the brother of Madar Sarder recorded his name along with, his relations instead of his brother. The defendants threatened the plaintiffs by virtue of that record and denied to effect partition which constrained the plaintiffs to institute the original suit. 

 3. The contrary case of the defendant No.5 who is the opposite party No.1 of the revisional application in short is thus that Bagan Behara Sarder was the korfa tenant under the original owner of the suit property Enamul Hoque Biswas. Due to arrears of rent a Rent Suit was filed by the landlord against Bagan Behara and the landlord obtained decree and in Decree Execution Case No.221 of 1952 the property was auction-purchased by the landlord. Thereafter, while the landlord proposed to settle the land, two brothers Madar Sarder and Nur Mohammad Sardar, son of Bagan Behara Sardar decided to take settlement and accordingly settlement was taken from the joint fund of the family and for joint interest of the family members but the kabuliyat dated 25.02.1956 was executed by the elder brother of the family Madar Sarder. The property was possessed in ejmali by two brothers and their mother and accordingly the S.A. record 602 was prepared in their names. At the demise of the brothers the property was devolved upon the heirs of two brothers. In this way the heirs of Madar Studer by way of inheritance acquired 27 decimals of land. During life time by two sets of kabla deeds Madar Sarder transferred 10½ decimals of land in favour the defendant No.5. The remaining brother Nur Mohammad by a registered kabla dated 09.08.1984 transferred his land in favour of the defendant no.5. The story of acquisition of the land by only one brother namely Madar Sarder is false and to deprive the other brother and his mother this was stated within the pleadings of the plaintiffs out of ill motive. The defendant not being the exclusive owner of 48 decimals of land have been owning and possessing that portion of land and the D.P. khatian accordingly prepared in his name. He has mutated his name and paying rent regularly. The plaintiffs on false allegation filed the suit which is liable to be dismissed. 

 7. The learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the learned lower appellate court during disposal of the appeal committed gross illegality resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in not taking the view that the settlement of the suit land in favour of Madar Sarder is genuine and that was for his own interest and money. The learned Advocate further submits that the kabuliyat which was a registered instrument in favour of the landlord was exclusively executed and registered by Madar Sarder and the learned District Judge have failed to appreciate the facts of the case including documentary evidence which is on records. There is nothing on record to hold such a view that the money for taking settlement was obtained from the joint fund of the joint family as alleged from the side of the contesting defendant. As a member of Muslim community there is no provision in the Mohammadan Law that joint family concept can be considered legal and as such the learned District Judge in taking decision over the pertinent point of the suit holding the view that as a member of a joint family for the interest of others Madar Sarder acquired the property is an error apparent on the face of the record. The learned Advocate also submits that the learned lower appellate court in his findings and observation once held that Madar Sarder as a member of joint family on behalf of his brother and mother and for himself obtained the settlement from the landlord and executed the kabuliyat but he has given a contradictory decision that the kabuliyat dated 25.02.1956 is an ineffective document and by this document nothing was accrued in favour of the plaintiffs. The learned Advocate submits that, Exhibit-3 is the kabla deed dated 31.10.1966 by which the two brothers namely Madar Sarder and Nur Mohammad Sarder sold land in favour of one Abdul Khaleque. From this kabla deed it appears that Nur Mohammad sold his land not from, the suit khatian but from different khatian and on the other hand Madar Sarder transferred his land from the suit khatian which proves that the settlement was taken by Madar Sarder himself for his own interest in respect of the disputed property. Besides this; the defendant no.1 who is the son of Nur Mohammad after giving evidence proved the case of the plaintiffs in taking settlement by Madar Sarder alone not with his brother Nur Mohammad which is not properly addressed by the learned appellate court below. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the plaintiffs paid rent in respect of the suit property till 1997 and taking advantage of wrong S.A. record the defendants mutated their names illegality and despite the S.A. record is not the document of title, the same is not properly appreciated by the learned appellate court and in this way the appellate court misdirected himself to the contents of Exhibit-3 the kabla deed dated 31.10.1966 and failed to assess other evidence on records in its true perspective. There is non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and as such the impugned judgment and decree is not sustainable. 

 10. On perusal of the case records it transpires that admittedly the property originally belonged to the landlord Enamul Hoque Biswas and Bagan Behara Sardar was a korfa tenant under the Ex-landlord. It is also an admitted position that there was an under khatian of the concerned C.S. khatian No.771 of suit mouza Madhabkhali and the area of the land was 54 decimals. It is also admitted that for arrears of rent the property was pot to an auction and the landlord Enamul Hoque Biswas auction-purchased the same. In a Rent Execution Case No.221 of 1952 the property which was auction-purchased by the landlord was proposed for settlement. It is the case of the plaintiffs that their predecessor Madar Sarder for his own interest and by his own money took settlement from the Ex-landlord and executed a registered kabuliyat on 25.02.1956. Vis-a-vis; it has been contended from the side of the contesting defendant-opposite party that after the death of Bagan Behara Sarder his two sons Madar Sarder and Nur Mohammad Sarder along with their mother were in a joint family and joint mess and it was decided by the two brothers that they would take settlement and accordingly on behalf of all the elder brother Madar Sarder executed the "kabuliyat" in favour of the landlord. Subsequently, during the S.A. record the elder brother recorded his name with his brother and mother's name in khatian No.602 which was finally published. In the instant case, the pertinent question which is the matter of adjudication is such as to whether the property is acquired alone by Madar Sarder or on behalf of all of the family members left behind Bagan Behara Sarder. It is a fact that the learned trial court during passing his judgment and decree examined six oral witnesses from the sides of the respective parties and decided the pertinent point in favour of the plaintiffs. Subsequently, the lower appellate court decided that the settlement in the name of Madar Sarder never effected and by virtue of that settlement nothing was acquired. Neither Madar Sarder nor Nur Mohammad Sarder nor their mother acquired any portion of land of the suit holding by virtue of the kabuliyat deed dated 25.02.1956 which has been marked as Exhibit-5 and Exhibit-`Ga' respectively from the sides of the respective parties. The proposition of law as cited with the recital of the impugned judgment and decree under the ambit of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act appears to be sound and cogent. Apart from this; the settlement followed by the kabuliyat marked as exhibit-5 was not completed as there is nothing to hold such a view that the Zaminder or the landlord ever obtained any salami or accepted rent from the settlement holder. Besides this; Section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1954 which takes it effect from 16.05.1951 have imposed a legal embargo in giving settlement by the landlord in favour of anybody. It has been properly appreciated by the learned District Judge, Satkhira in his findings. 

 11. Scrutinizing the corresponding C.S. Khatian No. 773 and its subsequent S.A. Khatian No. 602 it transpires that the land measuring an area of 54 decimals have been recorded in the name of two brothers and mother. It is on records that during the life time of Madar Sarder the S.A. record was not challenged by him and after his demise it has been challenged from the side of his successors the plaintiffs. It is a fact that during life time Madar Sarder by a registered kabla deed dated 31.10.1966 (Ext.-3) transferred some land in favour of one Abdul Khaleque and subsequently 19 decimals of land was transferred in favour of the plaitniff No.4 by a separate kabla deed dated 17.12.1990 and plaintiff No. 1 and 2 by virtue of their kabla deed acquired 19 decimals of land which has been properly addressed by the leaned lower appellate court. It is also not denied from any corner that in the year 1969 the predecessor of the plaintiffs Madar Sarder executed and registered two kabala deeds dated 10.06.1969 and 02.12.1969 which has been marked as Exhibits-"Gha" and "Uma". It is apparent from the face of the document that the kabla deed dated 31.10.1966 which has been marked as Exhibit-3 two brothers Madar Sarder and Nur Mohammad Sarder sold out some land in favour of Abdul Khaleque. From the contents of this document it appears that Nur Mohammad transferred different land with that of the suit khatian in favour of the purchaser and from the suit khatian Madar Sarder sold out some portion of land in favour of the purchaser. Apart from this; if we evaluate the oral evidence adduced from the sides of the respective parties we find that the plaintiffs in support of their respective case have examined three witnesses and the defendants in support of their case have adduced three witnesses. The plaintiff No.1 is the P.W.1 Abdus Salam Sarder. From his admission it has come to the notice of the court that his father Mader Sarder was aware about the S.A. record during his life time and he disclosed about the S.A. khatian before this plaintiff No.1. Hence; the learned appellate court rightly held that Madar Sarder during his life time did not raise any objection against the record of rights. Secondly; the plaintiffs relied upon the evidence of P.W.2 Abul Kalam who is the defendant No.1 to this suit. Admittedly, he is the son of Nur Mohammad and a man of 50 years at the time of giving deposition. In his averment he has stated that the plaintiffs do possess the suit land from 1990 and before them their predecessors possessed. Within his testimony it is apparent from his admission that he had no knowledge about the land prior to 1990. In the last portion of his deposition he has frankly conceded that he has no knowledge about the suit properties. The possession witness of the plaintiffs P.W.3 Khalilur Rahman tried to state in his examination-in-chief that he knows the suit land from the year 1990 and this land is being possessed by the plaintiff Salem, but scanning his cross-examination it transpires that he practically does not know the suit land. He admits that he has no land beside the suit land and he cannot say the boundaries of the suit land and also cannot say the quantum of the suit land. Under the ambit of sections 101 and 103 of the Evidence Act it is the incumbent duty of the plaintiffs that they are to establish their case by credible evidence, but in the instant case; it can be easily held that the witnesses those who are coming from the side of the plaintiffs are not competent and trustworthy and they have totally failed to discharge their onus in proving the case of the plaintiffs. Vis-à-vis; the oral evidence led from the side of the defendants go to show that the witness No.1 is the defendant No.5 himself who in support of his pleadings deposed. The other two witnesses Abul Hashem and Gobinda Chandra tried to corroborate the defendant No.5. The learned appellate court in his observation and findings assessed the evidence on records and rebutted the findings of the trial court adverting evidence.

Md Mokleshur Rahman, DAG with Farida Yesmein, AAG and Titus Hillol Rema, AAG—For the Respondents.

full_judgment:
Salma Masud Choudhury J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the enlistment of the property of the petitioner to the extent of his share measuring 12 decimals of BS Plot No. 157 appertaining to BS Khatian No. 9 recorded in the name of predecessor of the petitioner/ transferor corresponding to PS Plot No. 99 of PS Khatian No. 52 transformed from RS Plot No. 87/104 as appeared in item No.98 mentioning Plot No.9, Mouza Pahartali under PS Double mooring at page-15656(Kha) published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 26-12-1988 vide SRO 378-Law dated 25-12-1988 purportedly made under section 5(1) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Building (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance 1985 should not be declared to have been done without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. In the present Writ Petition the petitioner challenges the enlistment of his property appertaining to RS Khatian No.31, RS Plot No.87/104, PS Khatian No.52, PS Plot No.99, BS Khatian No.9, BS Plot No.157, JL, No.5, Mouza-Lot-9 Pahartali, Police Station-Double Moorings (Pahartali), District-Chittagong in the Kha(2) list as a supplementary to the Kha list of the abandoned properties published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extra-ordinary dated 26-12-1988 at page No.15656(Kha) against serial No.98 under the caption Plot No.9 Pahartali, Police Station-Double Moorings and the total area of 6.94 acres of land including the land in question appertaining to RS (CS) Khatian Nos.15 and 31 under Mouza Lot 9 Pahartali, JL No.5, Police Station- Double Moorings, District-Chittagong originally belonged to one Lalit Mohon Roy and others and in the RS (CS) operation the same was recorded in the names of one Amin Sharif and Serajul Haque as rayati tenants and thereafter the said Amin Sharif died leaving behind one daughter Sajeda Khatun as his sole heir and while enjoying and possessing the above land the said Sajeda Khatun transferred 1.12 acres of land including the land in question in favour of one Anwara Ahammad Chowdhury by a registered sale deed being No.2951 dated 16-4-1956 and delivered possession in favour of the transferee and was completely extinguished there from and after purchase, the said Anwara Ahammad Chowdhury, started enjoying and possessing the land peacefully within the knowledge of all and paid upto date land development tax to the government exchequer and during the BS operation, BS Khatian No.9 was correctly prepared and finally published in her name in 1987 and thereafter on 21-8-1994 at about 9-30 PM the said Anwara Ahammed Chowdhury died in Dhaka because of old age complications and during her life time Anwara Ahammed Chowdhury transferred the land in question measuring 12 decimals in favour of the petitioner by a registered sale deed being No. 478 dated 8-1-1985 and on delivering possession in his favour, became completely extinguished there from, and after purchase, while the petitioner started enjoying and possessing the land in question peacefully within the knowledge of all, on 1-3-2009, he went to the office of the concerned Assistant Commissioner (Land) for mutation but he came to learn that the land in question has been enlisted as an abandoned property vide the impugned Gazette Notification for which neither he nor his transferor Anwara Ahammed Chowdhury was given any notice. 

 11. The assertion of the petitioner that no notice was served at any time to treat the disputed property as an abandoned property, having not been controverted, we have no option but to hold that inclusion of the disputed property in the list of the abandoned properties published on 26-12-88 in pursuance of section 5 of the aforesaid Ordinance is without jurisdiction. 

 14. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The inclusion of the property of the petitioner to the extent of his share measuring 12 decimals of BS Plot No. 157 appertaining to BS Khatian No.9 recorded in the name of the predecessor of the petitioner/ transferor corresponding to PS Plot No.99 of PS Khatian No.52 transformed from RS Plot No.87/104 as appearing in item No.98 mentioning Plot No.9, Mouza-Pahartali under PS Double Mooring at page-15656(Kha) published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 26-12-1988 vide SRO No.378-Law dated 25-12-1988 purportedly made under section 5(1) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance 1985 (Annexure-B to the petition) are declared to have been made without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and respondent No. 1 is directed to exclude the property in question from the said Gazette notification dated 26-12-1988.

full_judgment:
2. The respondent Nos. 1-8 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 18 of 1997 in the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Kasba, Brahmanbaria, impleading the present petitioner as defendants and respondent nos. 9-22 as other defendant and respondent no. 23 as Preformat defendant, praying for declaration of title to the suit land and for recovery of Khas possession there-in alleging, inter alia, that the suit plot No. 638 and 639 along with on non suited plot no. 643 measuring 39 decimals of land originally belonged to Samena Bibi which was finally published in her name in C. S. Khatian and that the said Samena Bibi died leaving behind her only daughter Amena Khatun and thereafter Amena Khatun died leaving behind her daughter Malekernessa alias Melaka. While Melaka was owning and possessing the said plots she transferred the entire land of plot no. 643 by executing and registering deed of sale no. 3219 dated 26.4.62 and 07 decimals of land from the suit plots by executing and registering another deed of sale bearing no. 4967 dated 6.12.72 to the plaintiff no. 4 Abdul Sobhan alias Sobhan Miah. After purchase he mutated his name and got Jama separated in separation case no. 22483-84 by ' creating a separate Khatian no. 982 and took a loan from the Janata Bank, Brahmanbaria branch by mortgaging the said 07 decimals of land. Thereafter Maleka Begum died leaving behind one son Abdul Hossain, father of plaintiff no. 5, who died leaving behind plaintiff nos. 3-5 as his sons and daughter and thus the plaintiff nos. 1-4 became the owners of .27 decimals of land in the suit plot by way of purchase and by inheritance. It is further stated that in S.A. operation the suit property along with the property of plot no. 643 has been wrongly recorded in the name of one Aderjaman and other, predecessors of the defendants in khatian no. 117. The plaintiff learnt about the wrong record in the S. A. khatian on the basis of so-called partition suit no. 172 of 1929. The defendant no. 5 with the help of other defendants forcibly entered into the land of plot no. 638 on 30.9.96 and constructed two ducal tin shed and 3 chouchala tin shed defying the objection raised by plaintiff no. 3. 

 3. The defendant no. 5 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit is barred by limitation and that the suit plot no. 638 and 639 along with non suited plot no. 643 measuring an area of .39 decimals of land belonged to Samena Bibi and her name was rightly recorded in C. S. Khatian. Samena Khatun subsequently defaulted to pay rents and the Talukder was going to file a suit for realization of rent when Samena Bibi executed Istafanama deed dated 06.06.1920 and surrendered the property in favour of the landlord who settled the property to Munshi Mia son of Nawaj Ali on 10.09.1921 and thus Munshi Sheikh became the sole owner of the land of the said 3 plots and has been in possession of the said land and prayed for dis-missal of the suit.

full_judgment:
2. The plaint case, in short, is that the plaintiff instituted the Title Suit No. 230 of 1982 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Sadar Noakhali impleading the predecessor of the defendant petitioner and 3 others as proforma defendants for declaration of title of the suit schedule land of the plaint stating, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to Asshiny Kumar Chohoborti and Mohesh Chandra Chokroborti having 8 annas share each, Mohesh died leaving his only son Sheetal Chandra Chokroborti, Sheetal died leaving his only son Bushan Chandra Chokroborti as his heir. Bushan Chandra Chokroborti while owing and possessing of the suit land sold his share to plaintiff by registered deed dated 17-11-1972 and since purchase the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land. The plaintiff went to the Revenue Circle Office for mutating his name and came to know that defendant No. 1 mutated his name of the suit land by mutation in Miscellaneous case No. 540 and 537/72-73. The plaintiff also learned that one Devendra Kumar Chokroborti by kabala dated 18-1-1971 had sold the self same land in respect of schedule land to defendant No. 1 but Devendra Kumar Chokroborti had no title and possession in the suit land. During the period of MAR survey Devendra Kumar Chokroborti was a Peon of the local Tahshil Office and he must have included his name falsely in the MRR Khatian and such MRR khatian has created cloud in the title and possession of the plaintiff over suit land. Having learned about the wrong MRR Khatian on 2-3-1981 the plaintiff preferred appeal in the Court of additional Deputy Commissioner, Revenue but the defendant No. 1 fraudulently concealed the said appeal and thus, the plaintiff was constrained to file the suit. 

 3. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and stated, inter alia, that the plaintiff created the deed dated 17-11-1972 by showing false personation. Mohesh Chandra Chokroborti had no son namely Sheetal Chandra Chokroborti and Sheetal Chandra had no son namely Bushan Chandra and those alleged persons had no title and possession of the suit land but Mohesh had died issueless and as a result his brother Asshini inherited his share. Asshini died leaving his only son Devendra Kumar Chokroborti who became owner in possession of the suit land. Accordingly, MRR Khatian was finally prepared and published in the name of Devendra Kumar Chokroborti and Devendra while on owning and possessing the suit land by paying rent and taxes sold the suit land by registered kabala dated 18-1-1971 along with other lands to the defendant No. 1 and handed over possession and since purchase the defendant No. 1 has been owning and possessing the suit land by mutating his name, paying all rent and Taxes of the government and prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

 15. I have also found that the plaintiff has not made any pleadings/statements and prayer regarding the land situated at Begumgonj and also led no evidence in respect of the said land and the same has not been also brought in the schedule of the plaint. On perusal of the cross examination of the DW 1 as quoted above, it appears that the plaintiff gave suggestion about certain litigation of 1973-74 which clearly indicated that the plaintiff had knowledge about the MRR Khatian appearing in the name of the defendant in 1973-74 but the suit admittedly instituted in 1982 showing knowledge on 2-3-1981 and the evidence and suggestion has clearly indicated that the suit was instituted after about 9 years and thereby, the suit is barred by limitation. Admittedly, the property of schedule 2 and 3 of Exhibit 2 is situated under Noakhali Sadar Sub-registry office and in both the schedules the area is 0.70 decimals. The land shown in schedule 1 of the aforesaid Exhibit 2 is situated at Begumgonj and the sub-registry office is also at Begumgonj. On the scrutiny of the Exhibit 'Kha' (2) it appears that the land belonged to one Nim chand Raj but not to Sree Bushan Chandra Chokroborti and from the evidence it can clearly be inferred that the land shown in the Begumgonj PS is a fictitious land which the plaintiff has included in the schedule of Exhibit 2 kabala deed to get the deed registered in the Begumgonj sub-registry office, which apparently does not belong to Sr. Bushan Chandra Chokroborti. The plaintiff has failed to produce any document of Begumgonj that the land shown in the Exhibit 2 belonged to Sree Bushey Chandra Chokroborti nor any evidence is brought on record to show that the said land belonged to Bushan Chandra Chokroborti.

lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam with Mafuza Begum, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. 
Md Fazlul Karim with ABM Mahbub, Advocates ------ For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Nurul Haque (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Anowara Begum and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. Facts leading to the issuance of this Rule are that, one Mossammat Anowara Begum instituted the Other Suit No.18 of 1980 on 5-2-1980 in the Court of the Munsif, Thakurgaon, Dinajpur praying for setting aside the ex parte decree passed on 24-5-1979 in the Other Class Suit No. 100 of 1978 declaring the same illegal. collusive and not binding upon her and the learned Munsif by his judgment and decree dated 30-1-1982 has been pleased to decree the suit on contest with costs declaring the ex parte decree obtained by the defendant No.1, namely, Nurul Haque, on 24-5-1979 in the Other Class Suit No.100 of 1978 is not binding upon the plaintiff. 

 3. As against the said judgment and decree the defendants preferred the Other Appeal No.24 of 1992 and on 14-6-1984 the appeal was allowed by the learned appellate Court, by its Judgment and decree, setting aside the Judgment and decree of the learned trial Court and remanding the suit back to the trial Court with direction to the Learned Munsif to give an opportunity to the plaintiff to amend her plaint. On 25-2-1985 the case record was received by the trial Court from the appellate Court back on remand and the learned trial Court returned the plaint to the plaintiff for filling it before an appropriate Court and the 'plaintiff has re-filed it by amending the plaint in the Court of the Subordinate Judge. Thakurgaon and the suit has been registered as the Other Suit No.5 of 1984 and during trial of the case neither party adduced any additional evidence, but relied upon the evidence recorded earlier in the Other Class Suit No.18 of 1980. 

 4. On conclusion of the trial the learned Subordinate Judge. Thakurgaon has been pleased to dismiss the suit by his judgment and decree dated 28-5-1992 and being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiff has preferred the Title Appeal No.19 of 1992 and by judgment and decree dated 27-5-1993 the learned Additional District Judge. Thakurgaon, has been pleased to allow the appeal by setting aside the judgment and decree of the learned trial Court and declaring the ex parte decree passed in the Other Class Suit No.1 00 of 1978 on 24-5-1979. by the learned Assistant Judge, Thakurgaon illegal, void, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiff- appellant also declaring the title of the plaintiff in the suit property directing the defendant No.1 to vacate the suit land by demolishing and removing structures and declaring also khas possession of the plaintiff in the suit land on eviction of the defendant No.1 as aforesaid. 

 5. As against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Thakurgaon in Title (Other) Appeal No.19 of 1992 the defendant-respondent has preferred this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the instant Rule together with an order of stay of all further proceedings of the Title Execution Case No.5 of 1993 pending in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Thakurgaon. 

 6. Facts as appears from the pleadings of the parties and the judgments of the Courts below are that in the Other Class Suit No.18 of 1980 the plaintiff Mossammat Anowara Begum stated that the suit land originally belonged to one Subarna Probha Biswas and the CS Khatian No.420 was finally published in her name. Subsequently, the suit property was put to auction in the Certificate Case No.15311958-59 and she along with the defendant No.3 namely, Hanuman Das Agarwala purchased the entire land of the suit Khatian on auction held on 9-11-1959, with equal shares. The sale was confirmed on 9-1-1960 and they got delivery of possession of the suit land from the Court on 16-2-1960 and thus they acquired the right, title interests and possession of the suit land extinguishing the interests of Subarna Probha Biswas. 

 The defendant No.3 Hanuman Das Agarwala sold his half share to one Upendra Nath Barman who subsequently, filed a Partition Suit in the Court of Munsif: Thakurgaon, Dinajpur being No.143 of 1960 against the plaintiff and her husband and the suit was dismissed on contest. An appeal was preferred being Partition Appeal No.68 of 1961 and the learned Subordinate Judge. Dinajpur was also pleased to dismiss the appeal on contest. 

 Thereafter, Upendra Nath Barman again filed the Title Suit No.4 of 1963 in the same Court and obtained an ex parte decree on 2-9-1963. The present plaintiff, Mossammat Anowara Begum has then filed a suit for cancellation of that ex parte decree being the Other Suit No.37 of 1966 in the same Court and the said ex parte decree has been set aside and the original suit was restored to its original file and number and Upendra Nath ultimately, obtained a decree in that Title Suit. 

 The defendant No.1 has obtained an ex parte decree from the Court of the Munsif, Thakurgaon, in the Other Class Suit No. 100 of 1978 after he was defeated in the VP Miscellaneous Caseie after release of the suit property and got the ex parte decree behind the knowledge of the plaintiff, in respect of 19 decimal of land on 24-5-1979. The plaintiff was not made a party in that suit intentionally and her title has been clouded by that ex parte decree and thus, she has been obliged to institute the instant suit. 

 11. During the re-trial of the suit on remand, learned Munsif has framed two issues, namely, whether the suit is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and barred by limitation for the learned appellate Court has directed to decide those two points in its order of remand and the learned trial Court held that the plaintiff has proved her title in the entire land but the defendant No.1, Nurul Haque is in possession of 19 sataks of land and the plaintiff failed to prove that the defendant No.1 entered into the suit land' as tenant of the plaintiff. She did not produce any deed of tenancy agreement or rent receipts in this respect and her witnesses are partisan and their evidence are not reliable to the effect that the defendant No.1 entered into the suit land as tenant of the plaintiff. 

 12. On perusal of the document namely, the tax paying receipt of the Municipality of the year 1965, produced by the defendant No.1, the learned trial Court held that the defendant No.1 is in possession of that 19 sataks of land from 15/16 years ago. In accordance with the auction purchase dated 12-12- 1960. the plaintiff got possession in the southern portion or the suit plot and she could not explain as to how she got possession in 28'/2 steaks of land in the northern portion of the plot. By auction. Hanuman Das Agarwala got possession of this plot which he sold out to Upendra Nath Barman by a registered deed. Upendra Nath Barman instituted the Partition Suit praying for separate shaham where he lost upto appeal and, on the contrary, he won the Title Suit upto the appellate Court and in that Partition Suit this defendant No.1 was also a defendant. From that period this defendant is an illegal occupier in the suit land and his possession is adverse to all and continuous. The plaintiff has purchased from Upendra Nath Barman on 8-8-1970 by a registered deed measuring an area of 28-1/2 sataks in the northern portion of the plot but she could not prove acquiring her possession under the Kabala. The plaintiff also could not prove whether her vendor Upendra Nath Barman executed the decree which he obtained in his Partition Suit. The title of the plaintiff in the suit land is mere paper title and that she inserted her claim for recovery of possession on 29-9-1984 by way of amendment of the plaint. It could not be said that the possession of the defendant No.1 was not adverse to the plaintiff only because he took lease of it from the Government as Enemy Property. The defendant No.1 has enjoyed adverse possession and right, title thereof from 1963 to 1984. Though the ex parte decree was passed on 24-5-1979 in the Other Class Suit No.100 of 1978 without making the plaintiff a party and in her absence, but still it can be said that the decree was passed on finding his possession. The plaintiff has lost her cause of action by not suing from 8-8-1970. to 29-9-1984 and the suit is barred by section 144 of the Limitation Act. But the suit is maintainable in its nature and form. The suit is not hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. 

 14. The findings of the Learned Appellate Court in the Other Appeal No. 19 of 1992, on the contrary, are that as soon as the defendant No.1 took lease of 7 decimal of land from the Government as Enemy Property, his claim of adverse possession stood relinquished and, as such, the limitation of more than 12 years has been completed. The findings of the learned trial Court on the point of limitation was erroneous. The defendant No. 1 has not acquired any title by adverse possession and he is liable to eviction. The defendant No.1 claimed that he is dwelling in an area of 0.07 sataks of land having his dwelling house and possessing another 12 sataks of contiguous land by growing vegetables and plantation which is a new claim, not raised in the Other Suit No. 100 of 1978. 

 15. Mr Mahbubey Alam appearing with Mrs Mafuza Begum, the learned Advocates, for the petitioner, has advanced mainly threefold arguments: namely, (a) the plaintiff by adducing oral and documentary evidence could not prove the date of her alleged dispossession from the suit land. Relying upon the cases of Jogendra Nath alias Govinda Sarker vs Amulya Chandra Sarker and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 147. Abdus Sattar vs Abdul Rahman and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 100, the learned Advocate submits that since the plaintiff failed to prove induction of the defendant No.1 as her tenant in the suit land, he will be treated under the law, as a hostile possessor and his possession is adverse possession under the law; (b) With reference to the cases of Radhamoni Debi vs Collector and others reported in 27 Indian Appeals 136, Secretary of State vs Debendra Lal, reported in 1934 (Privy Council) 23; Ejas Ali Qidwai and others vs Special Manager. Court of Wards. Balrampur Estate and others reported in 1935 (Privy Council) 53 and Musa Ali vs Nur Ahmed and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 154 the Learned Advocate submits that since the possession of the defendant No.1 was open, overt, continuous and competitive against his competitor, the same has conferred a good title against all except the real owner and since the defendant No.1 has proved by evidence that he is in possession of the suit land the onus of proof was shifted upon the plaintiff to prove that he was inducted by her as her tenant or was her permissive possessor or licensee and in the absence of such proof: the possession of the defendant No.1 is clearly an adverse possession and (c) the defendant No.1 is in possession of the suit land from 1963 without break as it was found by the Courts below and so he has acquired his title in the suit land by way of adverse possession and the Learned appellate Court has erred in law in not holding title in the suit land by adverse possession and the findings and conclusion of the learned appellate Court is liable to be set aside. 

 16. Mr Md Fazlul Karim with Mr ABM Mahbub, the learned Advocates appearing for the opposite party, submits on the other hand, that the suit property was declared Enemy Property in the year 1969 and it remained as such till its release in favour of the plaintiff in the year 1978 and the defendant No.1 got lease of 7 sataks of land from the Government acknowledging and admitting the property to be the property of the Government and thus this period running from 1969-78 could not be added to or deemed to be hostile or adverse possession against the plaintiff. The learned Courts below found that the defendant No.1 has entered into an unlawful possession in 1963 and since the property was declared Enemy Property in 1969 his possession was of only 6 years prior to declaration of Enemy Property. The suit was instituted in 1980 and; as such, the period of his possession is not more than 8 years in all and, as such, he has acquired no adverse possession or title in the suit land. The plaintiff need not prove her constructive possession, since the possession of the defendant No.1 was broken. The defendant No.1 cannot claim his adverse possession in the suit land as was held by their Lordships in the case of Kumar Basanta Roy and others vs Secretary of Stale for India in Council and others reported in 44 Indian Appeals 104. 

 19. It has been variously described eg, (a) abnormal enjoyment. against all the world, but wrongly against the true owner (b) continuous possession against the title of the true owner if continued for the statutory period of limitation except making re-entry or bringing an action (c) Continuous exercise of right or title against the true owner which cannot afterwards be refused, either by re-entry or subsequent acknowledgment (Pannamma Velly vs Achu Thana Union. ILR 1966, 1 Kerala 689). Possession by continuous assertion against the title of the dispossessed owner and actual exclusive possession of the property commenced and continued to a clear right either openly or by a void claim' against a constructive claim adverse against the competitor and actual in continuity, in publicity and to the extent to show that its possession is adverse to the competitor. 

 23. In the instant case, admittedly the property belonged to one Subarna Probha and according to the plaintiff, the property was auction sold and she, together with one Hanuman Das Agarwala (defendant No.3) purchased that property in the auction proceeding and got possession thereof through the Court and subsequently, Hanuman Das sold out his share to one Upendra Nath who instituted a suit praying for his separate saham and he lost the suit upto appeal. He then instituted a Title Suit and obtaining a decree and won up to appeal. The plaintiff purchased the share of Upendra Nath, after being lost in that Title Suit and appeal, by her kabala and became owner of the entire property, in question. The case of the defendant No.1 is that the story of Certificate Case and Auction Sale of the suit property and purchase of the plaintiff are all false. Subarna Probha was the owner and possessor of the suit property and in the Khatian Hanuman Das was recorded as forceful possessor. When Subarna Probha left for' India sometime around the partition of the subcontinent, he got his possession in the property by making a house in the portion where Hanuman Das was the forceful possessor. Subarna Probha's property became Enemy Property and was listed as such in the year 1969 and he got lease of .07 sataks of land from the Government in whom the property was vested and in this area of land he has his homestead and the lease continued till its release in 1978. 

 The learned appellate Court found that the plaintiff's persuasion and chase to the equal share holder of Certificate purchase, Hanuman Das, has finally led to the point of her purchase from Upendra Nath. Upon purchase of the property in auction, the plaintiff got possession in the southern half and Hanuman Das in the northern half of the suit plot. While the plaintiff was trying to come to the northern half of the land in question by way of litigations with Hanuman Das he made an exit by way of transfer to Upendra Nath and Upendra Nath was in possession of this portion. From Upendra Nath the plaintiff has finally purchased it and Upendra Nath had his right, title and possession therein. 

 The learned first trial Court also found possession of the defendant No.1, but since the defendant No.1 could not explain his possession, the Learned Court held that it will not amount as hostile to the plaintiff. In the opinion of the learned remand Court, since before her purchase from Upendra Nath., the defendant No.1 was possessing the half share of Hanuman Das, so his possession was prior to the purchase of the plaintiff. It is hostile against Hanuman Das and also against the plaintiff. Though the plaintiff acquired title, but she did not get the possession of it. 

 In arriving at the aforesaid findings the Learned Courts below committed a grave omission in not looking into the fact, why Upendra Nath lost his Partition Suit upto its appeal against the present plaintiff and why he was compelled to institute a Title Suit instead: especially, why his prayer for separate saham was refused. 

 Send down the lower Court's Record at once.

caseno: First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 57 of 2002 with (Civil Rule No. 156 (FM) of 2002).
lawyer:
Mohammad Ali Khan, Advocate------For the Appellants. 
Arun Kumar Battachira, Advocate------For the Respondents.
parties:
Ershad Ali (Md) and another ------ Appellants
Vs.
Rampada Das & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Respondent No. 1 on 2-9-97 made an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 being Miscellaneous Case No. 25 of 1997 for pre-emption of transfer of the case land measuring about 2.89 acres of land appertaining to SA Khatian Nos. 589 and 596 fully described in the schedule to the application. The case was then renumbered as aforesaid Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 2000. 

 3. In the application, it is stated that SA Khatian Nos. 589 and 596 of mouje Helanchi under Thana Monirampur were recorded in the names of Eshan Chandra Das, Hazari Das, Rajbihari Das, Satish Chardra Das, Panchamoni Dasi and Sudhir Das in their specified shares. While jointly possessing his shares, Satish Chandra Das died leaving three sons, namely, the pre-emptor and respondent Nos. 2 and 3 (opposite party Nos. 4 and 5 in the application). 

 7. Appellants opposed the application by filing a written objection. They admitted that said SA Khatian No. 589 and 596 were finally published recording the names of said Ehsan Chandra Das, Hazari Das, Rajbihari, Satish Chandra Das and Panchamoni Dasi and Sudhir Das to the extent of their respective shares. 

 8. Their further case is that Hazari, Rajbihari and Satish Das got the interest of Panchamani Dasi, After death of Satish Das his interest devolved upon Rampada Das (pre-emptor). Shyamapada and Joyanta, and after death of Hazari Lal Das his interest devolved upon his three sons, namely, Durgapada, Shibpada and Kalipada. After death of Eshan Das his share devolved upon his wife Hazubala. Hazubala transferred 1.8425 acres of land to Sudhir Kumar Das by a deed dated 30-6-80. Sudhir Kumar Das got his name mutated in Miscellaneous Case No. 45/IX-I/79- 80 and No.317/ IX-I/82-83 and possessed accordingly. As Sudhir Das possessed his entire land inherited and purchased under khatian No. 1102 and the pre-emptor was not a co-sharer in such khatian the pre-emptor was not entitled to pre-empt the impugned transfer. 

 13. Upon the evidence oral and documentary on record learned Subordinate Judge found that the. pre-emptor was a co-sharer in the holding while the appellants strangers; the application for pre-emption was not barred by limitation and not bad for defect of parties; the appellants failed to prove their case that the right of pre-emption was barred by principles of waiver and acquiescence and the order dated 16-10-79 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 45/IX-I/79-80 opening new Khatian No. 1102 was not valid for want of service of notice upon Satish Chandra Das (father of the pre-emptor) and order dated 17-2-83 passed in 317/IX-I/82-83 did not, in fact, open any khatian, and would not be binding upon the pre-emptor. 

 16. Firstly, he submitted that in view of said orders passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 45/IX- I/79-80 and 317/IX-I/82-83 opening new khatians in the name of Sudhir Kumar Das in respect of his entire land and payment of rents on the basis of such khatian the pre-emptor was not entitled to pre-empt the impugned transfer since he was not a co-sharer in any of such holdings. 

 18. In the written objection, it is stated that Sudhir Kumar Das possessed his shares by separa- tion and amalgamation in Miscellaneous Case No. 45/IX-I/79-80 and under new Khatian No. 1102. Then, after purchase of 1.8425 acres of land from Hazubala he got his name again separated and amalgamated in Miscellaneous Case being No. 317/IX-I/82-83. Consequently, the pre-emptor who was not a co-sharer in such separated and amalgamated holdings was not entitled to pre-empt. 

 19. Appellant No.1 as OPW-1 deposed in support of such case. He said that appellant No.2 was his younger brother. Hazubala transferred 1.8425 acres to Sudhir Kumar Das. Sudhir Das got that land mutated in his name in Miscellaneous Case No. 317/IX-I/82-83. Sudhir Das also got his name mutated in Miscellaneous Case No.45/IX-I/79-S0. The pre-emptor was not a co-sharer in such mutated holdings. He did not see as to whether those mutated Khatians were mentioned in the impugned sale deed. He however denied that Sudhir Das did not file Miscellaneous Case No. 45/IX.-1/79-80 and obtained an antedated order therein. 

 20. Orders passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 45/IX-1/79-80 and No. 317/IX-I/82-S3 were adduced as Exhibit 'Ka' and 'Ka-1'. Four rent receipts were also adduced as Exhibit 'Gha' to 'Gha-3'. Of them, Exhibit 'Gha-2' and 'Gha-3' show payment of rents under impugned khatian No.1102. None of the rent receipts was proved by any witness. Even OPW-1 Ershad Ali in his deposition did not claim that Sudhir Das or anybody else ever paid rents under such Khatians No.1102 or 1134. 

 21. By ex parte order dated 16-10-79, Exhibit- 'Ka' the Circle Officer (Rev) at Manirampur allowed separation and amalgamation of said SA Khatian Nos. 589 and 596 and opened new Khatian No. 1102 in respect of 2.46 acres of land in the name of Sudhir Kumar Das. By another ex parte order dated 17-2-83 Exhibit-'Ka-1' the Circle Officer (Rev) purportedly again allowed separation and amalgamation of 1.8425 acre of land in the name of said Sudhir Kumar Das. But, in the orders space meant for writing Khatian No. and amount of rent is found vacant. No other evidence is found on record to prove that said Khatian No. 1134 was at all opened by said Circle Officer. 

 28. In the case ,before us we find there was an order passed by the revenue authority for opening a new khatian being No. 1102 in respect of 2.46 acres of land ata jama of Taka 4.30. As found already, the order was passed without any service of notice upon Satish Chandra Das, father of the pre-emptor. Moreover, no evidence could be adduced that such order and/or subdivision of the holdings was acted upon by the co-sharer tenants of the holdings. Payment of rents on the basis of such mutation Khatian by the co-sharer tenants over a period of seventeen year; could not be proved. 

 29. Last but not the least, vendor Sudhir Kumar Das transferred the land of Khatian Nos. 589 and 596 and the appellants purchased the same land of said holdings. Mere reading of the deed clearly evidences the intention of the appellants to purchase land of impugned khatians not new Khatian No. 1102. Now, sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act would not permit them to introduce any other intention of the parties to disentitle pre-emption.
